source: A Journey through every Billboard top 5 hit to find music’s greatest era
why: This states the project's goal, not a finding. The supplied files contain only chart dates, ranks, and song/artist metadata; they have no measure of musical quality or 'greatness', so no finding about the greatest era can be computed from them.

The page names 1997 as its opening case but never states a metric or result. The files only record chart dates, ranks, and song metadata; no chart-position summary is specified, and the obvious summaries do not put 1997 first (for example, it is not the year with the most top-5 hits, the most #1 songs, or the longest average #1 run). Choosing one summary to make 1997 rank first would be a definition the story does not use.

This loading-screen counter is a static placeholder that the JavaScript replaces from the data. In the files, the opening #1 (Wannabe) had a four-week run at #1 and MMMbop had a three-week run, so the displayed '2' is not reproduced.
This is a placeholder song label, not a finding. In the files MMMbop by Hanson reached #1 in 1997, not on the 1966 date shown beside it.

The files contain no chart date of 1966-08-21 (the chart weeks are Saturdays; the nearest is 1966-08-20), and the placeholder song beside it, MMMbop, charted in 1997. This label cannot be reproduced from the data.
This is a description of the source chart, not a finding. The supplied files contain positions only up to 19, not a full Top 100.

This is a description of the source data, not a finding. The supplied 2019 files cover chart dates from 1956 to 2019 and contain 3,034 unique song records (3,026 distinct track IDs in the weekly file), not 22,000 songs.
